sections.title: Who controls your face?
sections.narration: Do you choose your facial expressions, or do they choose you? Charles Darwin asked this in The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, published in 1872. Before him, many thinkers believed humans had been given special muscles for showing feeling. Darwin read the leading work of that view, by Sir Charles Bell, and said Bell's view, that man had been created with certain muscles specially adapted for the expression of his feelings, struck him as unsatisfactory. His doubt came from watching dogs, cats, infants, and people from many places. If expressions are tied to the body and its history, the story must be different. Imagine a flash of anger crossing your face in a meeting before you have decided what to say. Darwin wanted to explain why that happens. As we read, keep in mind that he worked with observation, letters from travelers, and photographs. Modern scientists have tested his ideas with new methods, and they have kept some and revised others. We will read him as a pioneer, not as the last word.

sections.title: Expression with a long history
sections.narration: Darwin's central move is to look at expression through the lens of evolution. He writes that he who admits on general grounds that the structure and habits of all animals have been gradually evolved will look at the whole subject of expression in a new and interesting light. In everyday terms, he is saying that a snarl, a smile, or a raised eyebrow may carry traces of older behavior. Our habit of reading a face is older than our reasons. Think of a person baring their teeth in rage. Darwin connects such a movement to the way many animals prepare to bite. This does not mean we are acting like animals when we are angry. It means that the same body has a history, and some expressions may be echoes of it. Scholars still debate how far this goes. Some modern researchers argue that many expressions are shared across cultures, while others stress that context and learning matter a great deal. The useful point is a modest one. Your face is connected to something older than your decisions.

sections.title: Habit leaves movements behind
sections.narration: Why would a movement continue after it stops being useful? Darwin proposes habit and association. He writes that whenever the same state of mind is induced, however feebly, there is a tendency through the force of habit and association for the same movements to be performed, though they may not then be of the least use. He gives everyday examples, such as a person leaning to one side while following a ball, as if the body could steer it. Most of us have done something similar. You wince during a movie scene though you are in no danger, or press an imaginary brake in the passenger seat. These actions once served a purpose, or seem connected to one. Now they simply accompany the feeling. It is a helpful way to understand your own reactions. When your body does something automatic in a tense moment, you do not have to treat it as a decision. You can notice it, and then choose what to do next.

sections.title: The dog and the principle of opposites
sections.narration: Darwin also noticed that opposite feelings often produce opposite movements. He calls this the principle of antithesis. His clearest example is a dog. When a dog approaches with hostile intent, its body takes a stiff, upright posture. When the same dog greets its master, it lowers its body and wags its tail in a loose, wriggling way. Darwin describes a dog whose attitude changed from joyful and dignified to downcast. He says every detail in its attitude was in complete opposition to its former joyful yet dignified bearing, and he explains it through the principle of antithesis. Notice the logic. A clear signal is useful because it differs from its opposite. People do this too. We open our hands and soften our shoulders to signal peace, and we square our shoulders to signal resolve. This is one of Darwin's more debated ideas, and later researchers questioned how widely it applies. Still, it is a pleasing way to see body language, as a set of contrasts we read without thinking.

sections.title: The blush and the watching mind
sections.narration: Darwin gives special attention to blushing. He calls it the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions. He also offers a precise claim about its cause. In his words, it is not the simple act of reflecting on our own appearance, but the thinking what others think of us, which excites a blush. Consider a moment when you realized someone had noticed a mistake. Your face warmed before you could decide how to react. Darwin's point is that the blush belongs to social life. In complete solitude, he says, the most sensitive person would be quite indifferent about his appearance. Modern psychologists generally agree that blushing is tied to social self-awareness, although the details are still studied. It teaches something kind. A blush does not mean you are weak, but that you care how you appear to others. When you see it in someone else, it may be worth responding with warmth, since they are already uncomfortable enough.

sections.title: Does showing a feeling make it stronger?
sections.narration: Here is a claim that anyone can test. Darwin writes that the free expression by outward signs of an emotion intensifies it. On the other hand, he says, the repression of all outward signs softens our emotions. He adds that he who gives way to violent gestures will increase his rage. Think of an argument in which raised voices make everyone angrier. Then think of a moment when you took a slow breath and relaxed your face, and the anger faded. Modern research on emotion regulation gives a mixed picture. Sometimes suppressing a feeling helps in the moment, but it can also cause strain, and expressing a feeling can bring relief or can inflame it. So Darwin's claim is not a simple rule. It still suggests a useful experiment for ordinary days. Next time you feel irritated, watch what your body is doing. Loosen your jaw, lower your voice, and see whether the feeling shifts. You are testing a nineteenth-century idea on your own mind.

sections.title: Expressions as messages
sections.narration: Darwin ends with a reminder that expression is not only a leftover. He writes that the movements of expression in the face and body, whatever their origin may have been, are in themselves of much importance for our welfare. He gives a simple example. A mother smiles approval, and thus encourages her child on the right path, or frowns disapproval. We have followed his main ideas: against special muscles, an evolutionary view, habit, opposites, the blush, and the effect of showing a feeling. Together they suggest that faces carry messages that work even when no one plans them. Remember what this book is. It is an 1872 study that relied on observation and anecdote, and later science has refined many of its claims. Read the original chapters yourself and notice where Darwin is careful and where he speculates. The useful ending is a precise question. Which expression of yours does the most communicating without your intending it, and what do you want it to say?
